news_drafts.headline: Lincolnshire forecasts a £54.071m high needs overspend, with its schools grant deficit rising to £54m
news_drafts.lead:
Lincolnshire County Council forecasts a £54.071m overspend this year on high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The figure is in the second-quarter financial review, which sits in the papers before the Overview and Scrutiny Management Board. It includes £34.541m that was already planned in the 2026/27 budget. The review says the dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools, is forecast to go from a £25m deficit to a £54m deficit by March 2027. It also gives a forecast overspend of £51.8m for schools revenue.

The paper says the £22.5m High Needs Stability Grant "does not address the ongoing in-year pressure". It puts the underlying high needs deficit at an increase of around £25m a year. The grant covers 90% of the deficit to 31 March 2026. The council's SEND Reform Plan forecasts a deficit of £57.8m for 2026/27.

On deficits arising after 31 March, the paper says: "Funding arrangements for deficits arising after 31 March are currently unknown". It records that government has said an appropriate and proportionate approach will be taken. Any residual unfunded deficit will need to be considered through future financial planning, the paper says. The reserves statement shows the DSG unusable reserve forecast at a £141.593m deficit in each year from 2027/28 to 2029/30.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix A - Report to Executive - Review of Financial Performance Q2

news_drafts.headline: Lincolnshire told of £22.5m grant covering 90% of its schools high-needs deficit after £23.0m overspend
news_drafts.lead:
Government confirmed in October 2026 that Lincolnshire County Council will receive a £22.5m High Needs Stability Grant to cover 90% of its accrued deficit on the dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools. The figure appears in the auditors' annual report for 2025/26 on the council's accounts, which goes to the Audit Committee on 16 November.

The council overspent the DSG by £23.0m in 2025/26. The report attributes the overspend principally to the high needs block, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities, and says this reflects a continued increase in children and young people requiring specialist educational support. The school budget deficit stood at £13.4m in 2025/26, against £2.4m in 2024/25.

The report notes that 2025/26 was the first year in which the DSG reserve was forecast to move into a negative position. It says that position was in line with the council's Medium Term Financial Strategy, which forecast a reduction in earmarked reserves. It also says the council had established arrangements to review high needs expenditure to mitigate the DSG deficit.

news_drafts.headline: Lincolnshire to bring in new special school funding bands from the autumn 2026 term
news_drafts.lead:
Lincolnshire's special schools will be funded under a new banding model from the autumn 2026 term, according to papers for the county's Schools' Forum meeting on 8 October. Banding sets the funding a school receives according to the level of need among its pupils.

The papers, an update on reforms to support for special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), say the review of the framework has been "progressed and concluded". The new model was developed with special school leaders and finance colleagues. It is meant to line funding up more closely with need, so that banding and funding "more accurately reflect need from the outset".

A key aim, the paper says, is to reduce reliance on exceptional funding arrangements, those that sit outside the standard bands. It also links the change to the long-term financial sustainability of the High Needs Block, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The papers give no figures for what the new model will cost or save.

findings.headline: The paper expects the 2026/27 pressures to continue into 2027/28 and beyond.
findings.detail: The paper says the same underlying financial pressures are expected to continue, and that the funding base for 2027/28 is largely fixed by the multi-year settlement apart from Council Tax flexibilities. The MTFP is being updated through confirm-and-challenge sessions with directorates during November.
findings.matters: A council stating that its funding base for next year is largely fixed, while expecting pressures to continue, is the position a lender and peers will read the budget-setting process against.
findings.figures: No figures for the 2027/28 gap are given in this paper.

findings.headline: Adult Care and Community Wellbeing forecasts an underspend of £2,109,276, attributed to a £2.1m reduction in the commissioned care budget.
findings.detail: The paper says stronger controls over commissioned care have supported a £2.1m reduction in the 2026/27 budget with spend remaining within the revised allocation. It also says strengths-based reviews and vacancies contribute to the position, but the paper describes these benefits as largely non-recurrent. The section heading gives a different figure of £2.051m.
findings.matters: A directorate that has cut its budget and met it while noting the savings are non-recurrent is a case peers can test against their own adult social care positions.
findings.figures: £2,109,276 underspend (Table 1); £2.1m reduction in commissioned care budget; £2.051m underspend (section heading); £1.573,301 Q1 variance
findings.quote: Strengthened controls over commissioned care have supported a £2.1m reduction

findings.headline: Resources and Corporate forecasts a £1.251m overspend, including the loss of a £0.948m carry forward from 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper says all service carry forwards, both overspends and underspends, were written off as part of the approved 2025/26 outturn treatment. The directorate therefore entered 2026/27 without the £0.948m that would otherwise have supported the budget. Legal Services is described as a key pressure due to locum reliance and recruitment difficulties.
findings.matters: The write-off of carry forwards on both sides is a specific treatment peers may need to consider when setting their own carry-forward rules.
findings.figures: £1.251m overspend; £0.948m carry forward lost; £0.4m deterioration in Governance; £0.254m improvement since quarter one
findings.quote: The forecast position reflects the loss of the £0.948m underspend carry forward from 2025/26

findings.headline: Other Budgets forecasts a £10.492m underspend, including £1.109m of pension contribution savings above the £9.006m budgeted.
findings.detail: The paper says the employer pension contribution rate fell from 24.1% to 17.8%, and that an exercise to recoup this saving from service budgets during quarter one realised additional savings of £1.109m. It offsets a forecast pay pressure of around £1m and a £0.533m mileage rate increase.
findings.matters: The pension contribution reduction is a one-off reallocation the paper describes, and a finance director elsewhere can compare how the national rate change flowed through to council budgets.
findings.figures: £10.492m Other Budgets underspend; £9.006m pension saving budgeted; £1.109m additional pension savings; 24.1% to 17.8% contribution rate; around £1m pay pressure; £0.533m mileage
findings.quote: The employer’s contribution rate to the pension fund reduced from 24.1% to 17.8% from April 2026,

findings.headline: Home to School Transport forecasts a £3.858m overspend at quarter two, up £0.174m since quarter one.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the pressure to growth in SEND transport, which is the costliest category, while overall passenger numbers have fallen 3.3% over three years. It reports an additional £2.474m pressure from the first month of the new academic year's costs, and says fuel inflation is well above the 3% budgeted.
findings.matters: The paper shows how SEND transport demand and fuel inflation combine on a fixed contract base, which is a common pressure for councils with rural networks.
findings.figures: £3.858m overspend; £0.174m increase from £3.684m at Q1; £2.474m additional pressure; £60.218m budget; 19,434 passengers budgeted; £16.48 average cost budgeted; £17.56 average cost forecast; 23.0% motor fuel price rise
findings.quote: Home to School Transport is forecasting an overspend of £3.858m at quarter two,

daily_post.headline: Paper states the underlying pressures behind the 2026/27 overspend are expected to continue into 2027/28 and beyond
daily_post.lead: A council stating that its current overspend drivers will carry into the next year, with a largely fixed funding base, is the kind of medium-term signal a finance director or lender would weigh against the MTFP.
